# 12-Week Upper-Body Programme
### Client Profile & Constraints Summary

**Client:** 29-year-old female | Recreational climber | Office worker
**Condition:** Right subacromial impingement (4 months post-diagnosis)
**Clearance:** Pain-free range only — **no overhead loading**
**Goal:** Rebuild shoulder health, restore balanced upper-body strength, return to climbing-ready capacity
**Setting:** Full gym access

---

> **Clinical Note for the Trainer:** Maintain ongoing communication with the client's physiotherapist throughout. If the client reports pain (>0/10 on any movement), stop that exercise immediately and regress or substitute. The programme deliberately avoids all overhead pressing, overhead pulling, and any loaded end-range shoulder elevation. Scapular control and rotator cuff integrity are the structural priority before any loading progression.

---

## Programme Architecture

| Phase | Weeks | Primary Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1 — Restore** | 1–4 | Scapular stability, rotator cuff activation, postural correction, pain-free movement mapping |
| **Phase 2 — Rebuild** | 5–8 | Hypertrophy and strength in cleared ranges, horizontal pulling dominance, grip and forearm work |
| **Phase 3 — Reload** | 9–12 | Progressive loading, climbing-specific pulling patterns, full upper-body integration |

**Session frequency:** 3 sessions per week (e.g. Monday / Wednesday / Friday), with active recovery on off days.
**Session duration:** 50–60 minutes.
**Session structure:** Each session follows — Warm-up → Activation → Main work → Accessory → Cool-down/mobility.

---

---

# PHASE 1 — RESTORE (Weeks 1–4)

## Phase 1 Goals
- Map the client's pain-free range of motion at the shoulder in all planes
- Activate and strengthen the lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior, and rotator cuff (particularly infraspinatus and teres minor)
- Correct the forward-head, rounded-shoulder posture typical of office workers and climbers
- Build a movement vocabulary she can trust before any meaningful load is applied
- Establish baseline grip strength and forearm endurance relevant to climbing

## General Phase 1 Notes
Keep all loads light to moderate. The emphasis here is on **quality of movement and neuromuscular recruitment**, not fatigue. Rest periods are short to moderate (60–90 seconds) because loads are low and the goal is motor learning. Every session begins with a thorough warm-up and ends with targeted mobility work for the thoracic spine and posterior shoulder capsule — two areas chronically stiff in climbers and desk workers alike.

---

## Week 1

**Objective:** Establish baseline, introduce activation work, build session habits.

### Session A — Monday

**Warm-Up (10 minutes)**
Begin with 5 minutes of light rowing on the ergometer at a conversational pace, focusing on a tall posture and a smooth drive. Follow with 2 minutes of thoracic spine foam rolling — place the roller perpendicular to the spine and work from T4 to T10, pausing at stiff segments. Finish with 3 minutes of gentle neck and shoulder circles, keeping all movement within a completely pain-free range.

**Activation Block (10 minutes)**
- **Prone Y-T-W raises** — 3 × 10 reps of each letter, bodyweight only, performed on a flat bench or the floor. The Y targets lower trapezius, the T targets middle trapezius, and the W targets external rotators. Cue the client to initiate each movement by "pinching the shoulder blades down and together" before lifting. Tempo: 2 seconds up, 1 second hold, 2 seconds down.
- **Sidelying external rotation** — 3 × 15 reps each side, using a very light dumbbell (1–2 kg). Elbow bent to 90°, upper arm pinned to the side with a small rolled towel between the elbow and ribcage to prevent compensation. Move only within a pain-free arc. This is the single most important exercise in Phase 1 for addressing impingement.
- **Serratus anterior wall slides** — 2 × 10 reps. Stand facing a wall, forearms resting on the wall at roughly chest height. Keeping contact with the wall, slide the forearms upward only as far as is completely pain-free (likely 90° or below at this stage). At the top of each rep, actively push the wall away to protract the scapula and engage serratus anterior. This is not a stretch — it is a controlled strengthening movement.

**Main Work (20 minutes)**
- **Seated cable row (neutral grip, elbows tucked)** — 3 × 12 reps @ RPE 5–6. Use a close-grip neutral handle. Cue a tall spine, retract and depress the scapula before pulling, and drive the elbows back to the hips. Avoid any shrugging. This is the primary horizontal pull of the programme and will be a constant across all phases.
- **Chest-supported dumbbell row** — 3 × 12 reps each side @ RPE 5. Set an incline bench to 30–45°. The chest-supported position removes lumbar stress and forces the upper back to do the work. Cue the client to lead with the elbow, not the hand, and to pause briefly at the top of each rep.
- **Dumbbell floor press** — 3 × 10 reps @ RPE 5. The floor press is the safest horizontal pressing option for this client because the floor acts as a hard stop, preventing the shoulder from going into the impingement-prone end-range of extension. Keep the upper arms at roughly 45° from the torso, not flared wide.

**Accessory — Grip and Forearm (10 minutes)**
- **Dead hangs from a low bar** — 3 × 20–30 seconds. Set a barbell in a squat rack at a height where the client can hang with feet on the floor, taking as much weight as needed through the legs. This is a decompression exercise for the shoulder as much as a grip exercise. Cue active scapular depression — "pull your shoulder blades into your back pockets" — rather than a passive hang.
- **Wrist roller** — 2 × 2 full rolls (up and down), light weight. Builds forearm endurance critical for climbing.

**Cool-Down and Mobility (10 minutes)**
- Doorway or cable pec stretch at 90° (horizontal, not elevated) — 2 × 30 seconds each side
- Sleeper stretch for posterior capsule — 2 × 30 seconds right side, 1 × 30 seconds left
- Child's pose with lateral reach — 2 × 30 seconds each side
- Thoracic extension over a foam roller — 2 minutes

---

### Session B — Wednesday

**Warm-Up (10 minutes)**
5 minutes on the stationary bike, followed by 5 minutes of dynamic mobility: arm circles in a pain-free range, scapular circles, and thoracic rotation in a seated position.

**Activation Block (10 minutes)**
- **Band pull-aparts** — 3 × 20 reps with a light resistance band. Hold the band at chest height with arms extended, palms facing down. Pull the band apart until it touches the chest, squeezing the shoulder blades together. This is a high-rep, low-load exercise — the goal is endurance of the scapular retractors, not strength. If the right shoulder reports any discomfort, reduce band tension immediately.
- **Prone cobra** — 3 × 10 reps, 3-second hold at the top. Lie face down, arms by the sides with thumbs pointing up. Lift the chest, arms, and head off the floor simultaneously, squeezing the glutes and retracting the scapulae. This is an excellent postural corrector for the office worker.
- **90/90 external rotation with band** — 2 × 15 reps each side. Stand side-on to a cable or band anchor at elbow height. With the elbow at 90° and the upper arm parallel to the floor (abducted to 90°), rotate the forearm upward. **Only perform this on the right side if it is completely pain-free at 90° of abduction.** If not, keep the right arm at 0° abduction (elbow at the side) and perform the same rotation pattern.

**Main Work (20 minutes)**
- **Lat pulldown to chest (wide grip, leaning slightly back)** — 3 × 12 reps @ RPE 5–6. This is a modified lat pulldown where the bar comes to the upper chest rather than behind the neck, and the torso leans back approximately 20–30°. This keeps the shoulder in a pain-free range while still training the lats and lower trapezius effectively. Monitor the right shoulder carefully — if there is any impingement sensation as the bar approaches the chest, reduce the range of motion.
- **Single-arm dumbbell row (knee on bench)** — 3 × 12 reps each side @ RPE 5–6. A classic movement that allows heavy loading in later phases. In Week 1, keep it light and focus on full scapular range — allowing the scapula to protract at the bottom and fully retract at the top.
- **Cable face pull (rope, elbows at shoulder height)** — 3 × 15 reps @ RPE 4–5. Set the cable at face height. Pull the rope toward the face, separating the hands at the end of the movement and externally rotating the shoulders. This is one of the most important exercises in the programme for shoulder health — it directly trains the posterior deltoid, middle trapezius, and external rotators simultaneously. Keep the load very light in Week 1.

**Accessory (10 minutes)**
- **Farmer's carry** — 3 × 30 metres, moderate weight. Grip strength, scapular stability, and postural endurance all in one. Cue a tall spine, depressed shoulders, and a controlled gait.
- **Pinch grip plate hold** — 2 × 30 seconds each hand, using a 5 or 10 kg plate pinched between the fingers and thumb. Directly relevant to climbing.

**Cool-Down and Mobility (10 minutes)**
Same protocol as Session A.

---

### Session C — Friday

**Warm-Up (10 minutes)**
5 minutes rowing, 5 minutes of thoracic foam rolling and shoulder mobility as per Session A.

**Activation Block (10 minutes)**
- Prone Y-T-W — 2 × 10 each letter (review and reinforce)
- Sidelying external rotation — 2 × 15 each side
- Serratus wall slides — 2 × 10

**Main Work (20 minutes)**
- **Incline dumbbell press (30° incline)** — 3 × 10 reps @ RPE 5. A low-incline press keeps the shoulder in a safer position than a flat or steep incline. The 30° angle reduces the impingement risk compared to a steeper incline while still training the anterior deltoid and pectorals. Monitor carefully.
- **Seated cable row (wide grip, elbows flared slightly)** — 3 × 12 reps @ RPE 5–6. A variation on the Session A row that targets the middle trapezius and rear deltoid more directly.
- **Chest-supported rear delt fly** — 3 × 15 reps @ RPE 4–5. Lie prone on an incline bench, arms hanging down with a slight bend in the elbows. Raise the arms out to the sides to shoulder height only — do not go higher. This is a pure posterior deltoid and middle trapezius exercise.

**Accessory (10 minutes)**
- **Dead hangs** — 3 × 30 seconds (progress from Session A if comfortable)
- **Wrist roller** — 2 × 2 full rolls

**Cool-Down and Mobility (10 minutes)**
Same protocol as Sessions A and B.

## Weeks 2, 3, and 4 — Phase 1 Progression

The session structure and exercise selection remain largely the same across Weeks 2–4. The progression is achieved through the following mechanisms, applied conservatively:

**Week 2:** Increase reps by 2 on all main work exercises (e.g. 3 × 12 becomes 3 × 14). Increase activation block sets by 1 where appropriate. Begin to challenge the serratus wall slides by allowing the arms to travel slightly higher if pain-free — perhaps 5° more than Week 1.

**Week 3:** Return to the original rep ranges but increase load by the smallest available increment (typically 1–2 kg on dumbbells, one plate on cables). Introduce **scapular push-ups** (3 × 15) as an additional activation exercise — these are performed in a plank position, allowing the chest to drop toward the floor by protracting the scapulae, then pushing back up by retracting them. This is a foundational serratus anterior exercise.

**Week 4:** This is a **deload week**. Reduce all main work volume by 40% (drop one set from each exercise and reduce load by 10%). Maintain activation work at full volume. Use the extra energy to focus on mobility, thoracic extension, and a detailed movement quality review with the client. Reassess pain-free range of motion at the shoulder and document any changes. This information will guide Phase 2 programming.

# PHASE 2 — REBUILD (Weeks 5–8)

## Phase 2 Goals
- Build meaningful strength and hypertrophy in the upper back, posterior shoulder, and arms within the established pain-free range
- Introduce more demanding horizontal pulling variations and begin to challenge the shoulder in slightly greater ranges where the physio and pain-free assessment permit
- Develop grip strength and forearm endurance to climbing-relevant levels
- Increase training density and introduce supersets to improve work capacity

## General Phase 2 Notes
By Week 5, the client should have a well-established movement vocabulary, improved scapular control, and a clearer picture of her pain-free range. Load increases become more deliberate here. Rest periods extend to 90–120 seconds for main work to support strength adaptation. Supersets are introduced for accessory work to increase efficiency. Continue monitoring the right shoulder at every session — progress is not linear with impingement, and some sessions may require regression.

---

## Week 5

**Objective:** Introduce Phase 2 loading, add new movement patterns, establish new baseline.

### Session A — Monday

**Warm-Up (10 minutes)**
5 minutes rowing at a moderate pace (aim for a stroke rate of 22–24 spm). Follow with band pull-aparts (2 × 20) and prone Y-T-W (2 × 10 each letter) as a combined warm-up and activation sequence.

**Activation Block (8 minutes)**
- Sidelying external rotation — 2 × 15 each side (now with a slightly heavier dumbbell than Phase 1 if pain-free)
- Scapular push-ups — 2 × 15
- 90/90 external rotation with band — 2 × 15 each side (reassess right side range)

**Main Work (25 minutes)**
- **Seated cable row (neutral grip)** — 4 × 10 reps @ RPE 7. Increase load from Phase 1. The additional set and higher RPE mark the shift toward strength adaptation.
- **Chest-supported dumbbell row** — 4 × 10 reps @ RPE 7. Same progression logic.
- **Dumbbell floor press** — 4 × 8 reps @ RPE 7. Reduce reps, increase load. Begin to develop pressing strength.
- **Cable face pull** — 3 × 15 reps @ RPE 5. Maintained as a health exercise — keep load moderate and focus on quality.

**Accessory — Superset 1 (10 minutes)**
Perform A and B back-to-back with 30 seconds rest between exercises, 90 seconds rest between rounds. 3 rounds.
- **A: Hammer curl** — 12 reps. Neutral grip targets the brachialis and brachioradialis, both highly relevant to climbing.
- **B: Tricep rope pushdown** — 12 reps. Elbow extension strength supports shoulder stability.

**Accessory — Grip (5 minutes)**
- Dead hangs — 3 × 40 seconds (progress from Phase 1)
- Pinch grip plate hold — 2 × 40 seconds each hand

**Cool-Down and Mobility (10 minutes)**
Same protocol as Phase 1, with the addition of a **thoracic rotation stretch in a half-kneeling position** — 5 reps each side, holding 3 seconds at end range.

### Session B — Wednesday

**Warm-Up and Activation (15 minutes)**
5 minutes bike, followed by the full activation sequence: band pull-aparts (2 × 20), prone cobra (2 × 10), scapular push-ups (2 × 15), sidelying external rotation (2 × 15 each side).

**Main Work (25 minutes)**
- **Lat pulldown to chest** — 4 × 10 reps @ RPE 7. Increase load from Phase 1. If the client's right shoulder has shown improvement in pain-free range, you may begin to experiment with a slightly wider grip to increase the range of motion challenge — but only if completely pain-free.
- **Single-arm dumbbell row** — 4 × 10 reps each side @ RPE 7.
- **Incline dumbbell press (30°)** — 4 × 8 reps @ RPE 7.
- **Chest-supported rear delt fly** — 3 × 15 reps @ RPE 5.

**Introduce: Inverted row (TRX or Smith machine)** — 3 × 10 reps @ RPE 6. Set the bar or TRX straps so the client is at roughly a 45° angle to the floor. This is a bodyweight horizontal pull that challenges the entire posterior chain of the upper body and is highly relevant to climbing. Cue the client to keep the body in a straight line and to initiate the movement by retracting the scapulae before bending the elbows.

3 rounds, same rest protocol as Session A.

- **B: Overhead tricep extension** — **Note: only perform this if the client can achieve the starting position (elbow pointing up, hand behind head) without any right shoulder pain. If not, substitute with a lying tricep extension (skull crusher) which keeps the shoulder in a neutral position.**

- Wrist roller — 3 × 2 full rolls

Standard protocol.

5 minutes rowing, followed by activation sequence.

3 rounds.
- **A: Incline dumbbell curl** — 12 reps. The incline position stretches the long head of the biceps, increasing the training stimulus — directly relevant to climbing.

Standard protocol.

## Weeks 6, 7, and 8 — Phase 2 Progression

**Week 6:** Add one additional set to all main work exercises (moving from 4 sets to 5 sets on primary movements). Maintain rep ranges. This is a volume accumulation week — the client will feel more fatigued than usual, which is expected and appropriate.

**Week 7:** Reduce sets back to 4 but increase load by 2–5% across all main work exercises. Introduce **cable woodchop (low to high, horizontal only)** as a rotational accessory exercise — this trains the obliques and serratus anterior in a functional pattern without overhead loading. Also introduce **face-down incline dumbbell shrug** — 3 × 15 reps — to specifically target the lower trapezius in a loaded position.

**Week 8:** Deload week. Reduce main work volume by 40%, maintain activation and mobility work. Conduct a thorough reassessment: measure pain-free range of motion, test strength on key exercises (seated cable row, lat pulldown, floor press), and review grip strength. Discuss with the client how her shoulder feels during daily activities and climbing (if she has returned to any light climbing). This assessment directly informs Phase 3 loading decisions.

# PHASE 3 — RELOAD (Weeks 9–12)

## Phase 3 Goals
- Achieve meaningful strength levels in all trained movements
- Introduce climbing-specific pulling patterns (scapular pull-ups, assisted pull-ups if pain-free range permits)
- Challenge the shoulder in greater ranges where assessment has confirmed safety
- Build the physical foundation for a return to recreational climbing at or above pre-injury capacity
- Develop the client's understanding of her own shoulder so she can self-manage going forward

## General Phase 3 Notes
Phase 3 is where the programme becomes genuinely challenging. Loads are meaningful, volume is high, and the exercises begin to more closely resemble the demands of climbing. However, the overhead loading restriction remains in place unless the physiotherapist has explicitly cleared overhead work by this point. The trainer should check in with the physio at the start of Week 9 and again at Week 11. If overhead clearance is granted, a conservative introduction of overhead pressing (e.g. landmine press) can be considered — this is noted below as a conditional addition.
